The lamellae's overtones are inharmonic: strongest at the attack and dying away quickly, they leave an almost pure tone, and neighbouring lamellae vibrate again in sympathy, adding harmonic complexity to each note. Traditional tunings often put the lowest note in the centre with the higher notes ranged on either side, and the seven-note series may span more than a Western octave, its intervals unlike Western equal temperament. 姆比拉又稱卡林巴琴，是源自辛巴威紹納人的撥奏體鳴樂器，屬簧片琴家族，Hornbo: The mbira, also called the kalimba, is a plucked idiophone from the Shona of Zimbabwe, in the lamellophone family, Hornbostel–Sachs 122.1. It consists of a wooden board, often with a resonator, carrying staggered metal lamellae; the player holds the instrument in both hands and plucks the lamellae with the thumbs and forefingers. Eastern and southern Africa have several kinds of mbira; they are often accompanied by hosho percussion and are used in religious rites, weddings and other social gatherings.
姆比拉常見於辛巴威紹納人的宗教儀式、婚禮與社交聚會，也用於稱為馬皮拉的聚會；在東: The mbira is common at the religious rites, weddings and social gatherings of the Shona of Zimbabwe, and is used at gatherings called mapira; in south-eastern Africa it often plays with hosho percussion. On the modern stage it can be used alongside the electric guitar, bass, drum kit and brass of a rock line-up while playing traditional repertory. It also appears in performance and teaching in North America, Europe and Japan, and has become a plucked idiophone of world-music settings.

The source notes that the lamellae were once made of bamboo and later developed into metal keys; some instruments have a resonator, but the source gives no material for it and says nothing about the other parts. The instrument sounds when the lamellae are plucked with the thumbs or fingers.

It sounds when the thumbs or fingers pluck the lamellae and set them vibrating; the usual way is for the thumbs and forefingers of both hands to work together. A beginner can pluck the lamellae one at a time at first, noting that neighbouring lamellae may vibrate again in sympathy. The source offers no fuller method, so only this basic order of operations can be described.

非洲撥奏體鳴樂器已有數千年；約三千年前西非海岸出現竹木彈片樂器，約一千三百年前尚: Plucked idiophones have been played in Africa for thousands of years: bamboo-and-wood lamellophones appear on the West African coast about 3,000 years ago, and the metal-lamella mbira in the Zambezi valley about 1,300 years ago. Metal-lamella instruments spread across Africa and developed different forms and social uses among the Shona of Zimbabwe and the peoples of Mozambique. In the mid-1950s the ethnomusicologist Hugh Tracey designed the kalimba on the model of the traditional mbira, which made it popular outside Africa; in the 1960s and early 1970s it was extended by Maurice White, Thomas Mapfumo and others playing it on stage with modern rock instruments.
